column2: The Threshold
The Monad, the Ineffable
Before the worlds, before time began to count, there was the One.
It had no name, for no one existed before it to name it; it had no measure, for nothing bounded it.
The Apocryphon of John calls it the Monad, the Invisible Spirit, Father of the All. The Valentinians called it the Depth, and its Thought, Silence.
It was not empty: it was a fullness so complete that it lacked nothing.
From it everything came — not by command, but by overflowing, like light that cannot contain itself.
Whoever wakes in the Kenoma wakes far from it. But not outside it.
Apocryphon of John (NHC II,1, 2–4); Irenaeus, Against Heresies I,1,1.
The Threshold, near the ashes of the awakening.
Torpor
The Pleroma and the Aeons
From the Depth and its Silence came Mind and Truth; from these, Word and Life; from these, Human and Church.
Each was an Aeon — not a place, but an age of the Light, a face of the Ineffable. And the Aeons came in pairs: the syzygies.
Thirty Aeons, said the school of Valentinus, and together they formed the Pleroma, the Fullness, where nothing sleeps and nothing forgets.
They were not made: they emanated, as heat emanates from fire.
The seven tiers you climb are also called Aeons. It is a parody.
Torpor is not an Aeon. It is what remains when an Aeon forgets itself.
Irenaeus, Against Heresies I,1,1–3 (the system of Ptolemy, disciple of Valentinus).
Torpor · Crossing I, at the rest between battles.
Sophia, Wisdom
The last of the Aeons, the youngest, was called Sophia: Wisdom.
For the Valentinians, she wished to grasp the Father alone. For the Apocryphon of John, she wished to bring forth without the Spirit's consent and without her partner.
It was not mere pride. It was love without measure: the longing to see the Source face to face.
From that unpartnered desire came something that should not have been. She cast it out and hid it in a cloud of light, a throne at its center, so no Aeon would see it.
The Valentinians told that, fallen, she wept: from her tears came water; from her laughter, light; from her grief and fear, matter.
Every torpor begins like this: someone loved so much they forgot themselves.
Apocryphon of John (NHC II,1, 9–10); Irenaeus I,2–4; Hippolytus, Refutation VI,29–36.
Torpor · Crossing V, before Athoth's antechamber.
Hunger
The Blind Abortion
Sophia's son was born misshapen: the look of a serpent and a lion, eyes like flashes of fire.
She named him Yaldabaoth. The texts also call him Saklas, the Fool, and Samael, “the god of the blind.”
Blind because he never saw the Pleroma his mother came from. Blind because he believed himself the only one.
“I am god, and there is no other but me,” he proclaimed. The texts answer: the boast is ignorance, not power.
He carried off a power of his mother's, and with it made a world by copying, blindly, the Pleroma he had never seen.
Hunger is the first sign of a blind god: he needs everything, and nothing fills him.
Apocryphon of John (NHC II,1, 10–13); Hypostasis of the Archons (NHC II,4, 87 and 94–95).
Hunger · Crossing I, just past the markets.
The Kenoma and the Hyle
Pleroma means fullness. Kenoma means emptiness: the deficiency, the lack.
It is not nothingness. It is a fullness that never satisfies: an endless market where no one is fed.
Matter — hyle — was born of Sophia's passions: of grief, of fear, of bewilderment.
“The lack came to be because the Father was unknown; once the Father is known, the lack is no more.”
Some texts despise the flesh and others treat it with pity. For the Valentinians, it holds a mother's grief.
Whoever eats in the Kenoma eats the shadow of bread. Whoever remembers has already tasted true bread.
Irenaeus I,4–5; Gospel of Truth (NHC I,3, 24–25).
Hunger · The Challenge, at the Champion's shrine.
The Seven Archons and the Spheres
Yaldabaoth begot rulers — Archons — in his own likeness, and set seven kings over the seven heavens.
The ancients linked the seven heavens to the seven wandering stars, from the Moon to Saturn.
Athoth, Harmas, Galila, Yabel, Belias and Armupiel come from the Apocryphon of John's list of authorities; Astaphaios, from the list of the seven kings.
In the texts, each receives a power. Here, each door exacts a passion: sleep, hunger, law, silence, reflection, rot, crown.
In the Hermetic Poimandres, the rising soul gives back one vice to each sphere, until it reaches the eighth, free.
They are not demons. They are officials of a deception — and every official dreams of the boss's seat.
Apocryphon of John (NHC II,1, 10–12; BG 8502,2); Origen, Against Celsus VI,31; Poimandres (Corpus Hermeticum I,25–26).
Hunger · Crossing V, past the shrine.
Chain
Heimarmene, Fate in Chains
The Archons begot Fate — Heimarmene — and bound it to the stars.
Every birth under a sign; every life in an orbit; every death on the appointed day.
The Apocryphon calls it the harshest of fetters: by it gods, angels, demons and humans were bound to measures, seasons and times.
“Until baptism, Fate holds true; after it, the astrologers no longer get it right,” Theodotus taught.
Gnosis does not deny the stars. It denies that they have the last word.
The law of this Aeon is that chain: beautiful, polished — and still a chain.
Apocryphon of John (NHC II,1, 28); Clement of Alexandria, Excerpts from Theodotus 69–78.
Chain · Crossing I, past the first seals.
The Man of Clay and the Spark
The image of the perfect Human shone on the waters below, and the Archons wished to copy it: “Let us make a man after the image of God and in our own likeness.”
They shaped him, but he would not rise: he lay on the ground, motionless, soulless. Other accounts say he crawled like a worm.
Then the Light acted by cunning: it made the Blind One breathe into the man's face the power he had taken from his mother.
And the man rose, more luminous than his makers. The Archons grew envious and cast him down into the depths of matter.
Every person carries that spark: a piece of the Light the jailer did not want to give, and gave.
The chain binds the clay. It never bound the spark.
Apocryphon of John (NHC II,1, 14–21); Hypostasis of the Archons (NHC II,4, 87–88); Irenaeus I,24,1 (Saturninus).
